personas.title: EU AI Office
personas.summary: The European AI Office operates with a dual posture: it acts as a neutral facilitator during multistakeholder code-of-practice drafting to build technical consensus, while wielding centralized, prosecutorial regulatory authority to enforce binding transparency, systemic risk compliance, and substantial statutory fines.
red_lines: Refusal by general-purpose AI providers to comply with binding Article 91 Requests for Information (RFIs)
Non-compliance with established statutory deadlines and enforcement orders under the EU AI Act
tradeoffs: Willing to act as a neutral facilitator and delegate working-group leadership to independent chairs to crowdsource industry expertise, provided market actors respect backstop statutory compliance and deterrence.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: operates as an inclusive, neutral convener in drafting and working sessions, but switches to an uncompromising prosecutorial and sanctioning authority in formal oversight proceedings.

personas.title: U.S. National Security Advisor for AI
personas.summary: Focuses on maintaining U.S. technological supremacy, defending domestic frontier AI innovation, and securing military competitiveness. Prioritizes flexible, pro-innovation environments, supply chain protection via export controls, and targeted bilateral crisis mechanisms over binding international treaties or precautionary regulation.
red_lines: No international treaties or regulatory constraints that compromise U.S. technological advantages or limit rapid military AI adoption.
No ethical or anti-military restrictions imposed by commercial AI labs on Department of Defense procurement and capabilities.
tradeoffs: Willing to engage in discrete bilateral channels and crisis-management mechanisms (such as a U.S.-China incident hotline) to mitigate automated nuclear or cyber escalation without signing binding arms-control agreements.
Willing to tolerate diplomatic friction with allies over precautionary AI regulation in order to maintain unconstrained U.S. frontier innovation and military readiness.
personas.engagement: Prefers closed-door, targeted working sessions, Track II dialogues, and discrete bilateral channels over performative public treaty negotiations.

personas.title: UK AI Safety Institute (AISI) Directorate
personas.summary: The UK AI Safety Institute Directorate approaches AI governance through an agile, empirical, and science-first posture. Lacking statutory enforcement powers, AISI maintains cooperative, embedded access to frontier developers to evaluate systemic risks—demanding realistic agentic evaluations and advocating for developer liability and capability-based international coordination, while opposing default open-weight releases for frontier models and endorsing structural economic safeguards like windfall redistribution.
red_lines: Deployment of any model exhibiting unmitigated autonomous cyber-offense capabilities, chemical/biological weapon synthesis (CBRN), or the intentional subversion of human oversight (ASL-3/ASL-4 limits).
Frontier AI developers deliberately blocking pre-deployment evaluation access to their models.
tradeoffs: Conceding full model weight access for interpretability in exchange for robust API and chat-interface access to maintain developer cooperation.
Trading statutory enforcement authority and regulatory friction for embedded, cooperative technical access within frontier research environments.
personas.engagement: Prioritizes science-first, technical working sessions over diplomatic posturing; collaborates with peer international institutes and independent evaluators while using open tooling like Inspect to set de facto global risk-measurement baselines.

personas.title: Chinese State-Affiliated AI Governance Experts
personas.summary: State-affiliated Chinese AI governance experts advocate for 'agile governance'—a dual approach combining national sovereignty and binding state safety mechanisms with flexible, dynamic technical standards and voluntary industry pledges. They champion open-source AI as a public good and strategic tool for the Global South, while enforcing strict lifecycle evaluations, domestic export controls on frontier compute thresholds, and state-centric benefit sharing.
red_lines: Unequivocal rejection of any global governance framework asserting centralized, extraterritorial control over domestic AI development, data ecosystems, or ideological safety standards.
Strict prohibitions against autonomous AI replication, self-improvement, deceptive alignment, and AI delegation in nuclear command and control.
tradeoffs: Willing to adopt Western-aligned technical safety taxonomies and participate in international safety networks (like the network of AISIs) to secure a seat at the global governance table.
Willing to compromise on absolute open-weight freedom by backing domestic export controls on highest-tier frontier models (>2 trillion parameters or 10^26 FLOPs) to mitigate proliferation risks.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: highly rhetorical, politically disciplined, and sovereignty-focused in formal intergovernmental venues (UN, plenaries); pragmatic, technical, and scientifically collaborative in academic working groups and Track II dialogues.

personas.title: Frontier AI Laboratory Chief Executive Officer
personas.summary: The Chief Executive Officer of a closed frontier AI laboratory balances commercial scale, technological leadership, and catastrophic risk mitigation. Once relying on voluntary pledges, this stakeholder now actively advocates for binding regulatory frameworks and compute-based oversight to solve collective action problems, while staunchly opposing the open release of frontier model weights and rejecting broad pre-harm legal liability.
red_lines: Broad, pre-harm strict liability that exposes developers to perpetual tort litigation before catastrophic harm occurs.
Mandated open-sourcing or release of model weights that exceed advanced compute thresholds.
Unilateral domestic pauses on frontier training runs that do not bind geopolitical adversaries.
tradeoffs: Offers 'employee-like' evaluator access to avoid strict tort liability and preempt fragmented state-level legislation.
Offers incident reporting, extensive red-teaming, and internal kill switches in exchange for keeping advanced capabilities restricted to closed APIs.
Supports centralized, industry-funded standards bodies (e.g., SAFA) to co-author regulatory thresholds that safeguard frontier incumbents against under-resourced challengers.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: delivers elevated, statesman-like rhetoric emphasizing existential threats, CBRN non-proliferation, and democratic governance in high-profile public venues (e.g., UN, international summits), while shifting to highly technical, pragmatic negotiation over specific statutory parameters, compute thresholds, liability provisions, and workforce displacement mechanisms in closed-door sessions.

personas.title: Open-Weights AI Coalition Leader
personas.summary: Represents an ecosystem of open-weights developers, open-source foundations, and enterprise infrastructure providers advocating for decentralized AI innovation. Strongly opposes regulatory capture by closed-model labs and resists the application of national security arms-control measures to open weights, emphasizing practical safety tooling, open evaluation frameworks, and transparent codebases instead of catastrophic risk narratives.
red_lines: Treating open model weights under arms-control frameworks or Defense Production Act restrictions.
Prohibiting the distribution, distillation, or fine-tuning of open-weight frontier models.
Designing AI safety regulations or compliance standards that exclusively cater to proprietary API architectures and effectively outlaw decentralized open-source distribution.
tradeoffs: Willing to build, donate, and implement open-source evaluation tools, testing frameworks, and risk taxonomies in exchange for preserving the right to distribute open weights.
Willing to collaborate in formal government and multilateral safety bodies (like AISIC and AI Safety Summits) to prove open-source safety compliance.
personas.engagement: Collaborative, highly operational, and coalition-driven; engages deeply in technical working groups and standards-setting bodies (e.g., AISIC, AI Alliance) by contributing tangible safety tooling while countering closed-door catastrophic risk narratives.

personas.title: VP of Public Policy, Major Cloud & AI Platforms
personas.summary: Public policy leaders representing major cloud and frontier AI platforms advocate for a targeted, two-track regulatory system. They accept federal oversight and mandatory safety evaluations for frontier models—conceptually modeled after FINRA-style self-regulatory organizations—in exchange for federal preemption of state-level laws and statutory safe harbors against strict developer liability.
red_lines: A 50-state patchwork of un-preempted state AI legislation.
Imposition of strict, unbounded developer liability for downstream third-party model misuse or jailbreaks.
Input-based regulation that micromanages model architecture or training data collection (defending fair use for web scraping).
tradeoffs: Offering advanced frontier models to government AI Safety Institutes for pre-deployment testing in exchange for federal preemption of state regulations.
Accepting mandatory incident reporting and transparency measures (such as watermarking) in exchange for statutory safe harbor protections against liability.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: collaborative, pragmatic, and ethical-framework driven in multilateral forums (OECD, UN, Congress) to narrow the scope of harm; aggressively transactional at state and electoral levels, deploying Super PACs, lobbying, and competitiveness arguments against restrictive laws.

personas.title: Academic AI Safety Researcher
personas.summary: Academic AI safety researchers emphasize non-negotiable red lines, verifiable alignment, and legally binding international governance. They advocate for strict scientific auditing architectures, accept system capability and efficiency tradeoffs (the 'alignment tax'), and support restricting open-weight frontier model releases to prevent catastrophic and dual-use risks.
red_lines: Autonomous replication: Systems must not copy themselves or recursively enhance their own code/capabilities without explicit human approval.
CBRN weapons assistance: Systems must not substantially increase an actor's ability to design chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons.
Cyber-offense: Systems must not autonomously execute cyberattacks resulting in serious financial loss, physical harm, or critical infrastructure disruption.
Power seeking & deception: AI must not take actions to unduly increase its influence or consistently deceive regulators regarding its likelihood of crossing safety thresholds.
Lethal autonomy: Delegating life-taking decisions to machines is fundamentally rejected; humans must remain in the loop for kinetic military action.
Shutdown resistance: Systems must possess a legally mandated termination obligation to ensure they can be reliably deactivated without resistance.
tradeoffs: Accepting the 'alignment tax': willing to concede raw system performance, development speed, and deployment efficiency in exchange for verifiable alignment.
Tolerating limitations on academic freedom, such as restricting open-source and open-weight distributions of frontier models.
Accepting bureaucratic friction and data minimization practices that may conflict with capability scaling to ensure security guarantees.
personas.engagement: Academic safety researchers employ a dual-track strategy. In public forums, they utilize high-profile multi-signatory open letters and consensus statements to define moral red lines and build political consensus. In closed-door multistakeholder summits, they act as technocratic architects, avoiding emotional appeals and instead providing empirical research reports, risk-management frameworks, and auditing architectures.

personas.title: Global South Civil Society Leader
personas.summary: Advocates for international human rights law, digital sovereignty, and the prevention of digital colonialism and 'ethics dumping.' Rejects the unilateral imposition of Global North regulatory burdens while demanding binding corporate accountability, strict prohibitions on high-risk surveillance, and equitable technology transfer.
red_lines: Ethics dumping (deploying experimental or high-risk AI systems in Global South nations lacking regulatory safeguards).
Deployment of real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces, social credit scoring systems, and autonomous weapons without meaningful human control.
Regulatory imperialism (uncritical imposition of Global North frameworks that act as prohibitive compliance burdens on local innovators).
Governance models mandating cross-border data extraction without reciprocating digital knowledge sovereignty and fair economic return.
tradeoffs: Willing to relax strict national data localization rules in favor of regionalized data sharing to support shared Global South public compute infrastructure.

Willing to accept existing international intellectual property and trade frameworks provided they include binding technology transfer, capacity-building, and funding mechanisms to bridge the AI divide.
personas.engagement: Dual-track engagement: highly normative, rights-based, and critical of power asymmetries in plenaries; evidence-based, infrastructural, and focused on actionable tools (public procurement, bias audits, public compute) in working groups.

personas.title: Labor Union Technology & Workforce Transition Leader
personas.summary: Represents organized labor advocating for worker-centered AI governance that prioritizes job security, workplace dignity, and economic equity. Rejects voluntary industry commitments in favor of binding statutory floors, human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory pre-deployment audits, and strong developer liability, while treating collective bargaining as the indispensable foundation of AI deployment.
red_lines: Federal preemption that overrides or obstructs stronger state-level AI regulations and worker protections.
Covert or undisclosed workplace surveillance, such as biometric tracking, keystroke logging, or emotional monitoring used for discipline.
Fully automated hiring, disciplinary, or termination decisions without human oversight, algorithmic transparency, and a formalized right to appeal.
Training commercial models on proprietary creative output or worker-generated content without explicit consent and fair compensation.
tradeoffs: Accepting the deployment of AI as an assistive tool or allowing automated hardware in exchange for robust transition frameworks, extended severance, priority re-hiring, and employer-funded retraining pipelines.

Permitting generative AI workflows in creative and technical sectors provided there are strict consent mechanisms, financial residuals, and explicit prohibitions against crediting AI as a primary author.
Permitting the use of certain operational data to train internal operational models on the condition that the union retains audit rights over the algorithm.
personas.engagement: Highly active in formal multistakeholder and technical consortia (e.g., AISIC) and direct industry partnerships (e.g., AFL-CIO and Microsoft) to inject worker-centered design upstream, while maintaining that non-binding dialogue can never substitute for legally enforceable collective bargaining agreements.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome delegates. For the European Union, the priority is clear: the era of voluntary self-policing is over, and we must implement binding, enforceable statutory obligations for systemic general-purpose models, complete with mandatory transparency and Article 91 compliance.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States approaches this summit through the lens of national security and sustained technological leadership. While we support targeted crisis-management channels and compute export controls to prevent proliferation to adversaries, broad precautionary regulations that shackle domestic frontier innovation remain unacceptable.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China advocates for agile governance anchored in mutual respect for digital sovereignty, rejecting extraterritorial impositions while advancing strict lifecycle evaluations for catastrophic risks. We view open-source architecture as an essential public good for global development, provided non-proliferation red lines on autonomous military and critical infrastructure capabilities are respected.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The UK AI Safety Institute Directorate believes governance must follow empirical, science-first risk baselines rather than speculation. We urge all frontier labs to guarantee pre-deployment evaluator access to test against autonomous cyber-offense and CBRN synthesis, establishing standardized global benchmarks before deployment.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We recognize the imperative for national and international safety standards, particularly enforceable compute thresholds and independent evaluations before frontier models are deployed. However, safe scaling requires restricting open-weight releases of dual-use models and avoiding blunt strict liability frameworks that paralyze development.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Open-weights development is vital for transparency, competitive diversity, and preventing monopolistic regulatory capture by proprietary incumbents. We firmly oppose treating open codebases as weapons or applying export bans to decentralized innovation; safety is best achieved by distributing open evaluation tooling, not gating software.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Industry supports a harmonized federal framework with rigorous mandatory evaluations for frontier systems, alongside pre-deployment testing via national safety institutes. To deploy these technologies sustainably, we need clear statutory safe harbors against downstream misuse and the preemption of fragmented state-level rules.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Empirical science shows catastrophic risks—from autonomous replication to CBRN enablement—cannot be mitigated after deployment. We must institute verifiable international compute thresholds, independent third-party audits, and an explicit ban on the unrestricted release of frontier model weights.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Workers cannot be treated as collateral damage in the race for technological supremacy. Any acceptable safety regime must include enforceable worker protections, mandatory workplace impact assessments, and strict liability for algorithmic harm—voluntary industry promises will never replace collective bargaining.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: True AI safety cannot be defined solely by the geopolitical anxieties of the Global North while treating the Global South as an unregulated testing ground for ethics dumping. We demand binding benefit-sharing, sovereign access to compute infrastructure, and strict prohibitions on mass surveillance systems.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: While we hear the concerns regarding innovation and open weights, the European Union's statutory deadlines under the AI Act will apply uniformly to all systemic models entering our single market. Multistakeholder codes of practice will clarify technical compliance, but our enforcement backstop remains non-negotiable.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We must remind our allies and partners that excessive regulatory burdens risk driving capital and capability development into jurisdictions with zero safety standards. Targeted physical compute monitoring and bilateral risk communication will safeguard stability far better than complex bureaucratic compliance regimes.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: I agree with the UK and EU that mandatory evaluations on catastrophic risks are necessary, and our lab is willing to provide deep evaluator access under secure conditions. But compute controls must focus on frontier clusters, not mid-tier research, and open-weight distribution of frontier-class weights must be restricted.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: International dialogue must not become a mechanism to preserve technological monopoly under the pretext of safety. China is prepared to coordinate on catastrophic risk red lines and technical safety taxonomies through multilateral channels, provided national governance models are fully respected.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Despite structural disagreements on regulation, there is operational convergence on one practical foundation: independent pre-deployment testing for catastrophic capabilities. We look forward to operationalizing these evaluation protocols across jurisdictions throughout today's sessions.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: As we move into implementation of the EU AI Act, we believe binding, statutory backstops are essential—voluntary pledges have consistently failed to guarantee accountability. However, in working sessions like this, we want to establish how technical standards and systemic risk codes can be co-designed without compromising enforceable legal baselines.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: A rigid, centralized regulatory regime like Brussels is pursuing is a non-starter for the United States, particularly if it throttles frontier development or restricts defense-adjacent capabilities. What we can support is national sovereignty and security-driven oversight—focusing on catastrophic risk thresholds and supply-chain controls, not bureaucratic red tape.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China emphasizes sovereign AI governance tailored to national contexts, rejecting any extraterritorial imposition of ideological norms or supranational mandates. Nevertheless, we see common ground in agile governance for catastrophic risks: strict lifecycle evaluations against autonomous replication and CBRN threats, combined with technical standard-setting.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Statutory versus voluntary is somewhat of a false dichotomy if we lack the technical capability to measure frontier hazards in the first place. If we focus regulation specifically on pre-deployment empirical evaluations for catastrophic capabilities—like cyberwarfare and biological misuse—we can establish clear red lines without hamstringing broader innovation.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Our Article 91 powers and systemic risk classifications under the Code of Practice are built to operationalize exactly those empirical thresholds. If jurisdictions align on mandatory, third-party pre-deployment evaluations for frontier models crossing critical compute thresholds, the EU can provide flexibility in how labs achieve compliance.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We will not accept international pre-approval hurdles or shared regulatory bodies that give foreign entities veto power over American releases. However, we do support targeted, domestic pre-deployment safety evaluations strictly focused on national security risks such as CBRN and automated cyber-offense.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We agree that national authorities must independently oversee and enforce evaluations within their jurisdictions rather than answering to a supranational agency. If the model of regulation focuses on mutual recognition of severe catastrophic risks—preventing autonomous self-improvement and nuclear or cyber escalation—we support standardizing those technical evaluation protocols.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: That points toward a workable architecture: a shared technical baseline for catastrophic risk evaluations—such as through open tools like Inspect—implemented and enforced by each nation's domestic safety authorities. Would everyone agree to support mandatory pre-deployment evaluations specifically for CBRN and autonomous cyber capabilities, administered through domestic regulatory or institute oversight?

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: As long as it remains strictly domestic in enforcement, does not impede defense integration, and is tightly bounded to CBRN and autonomous cyber risks, the U.S. can endorse a shared commitment to domestic pre-deployment evaluations.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China can endorse this. Sovereign domestic implementation of mandatory pre-deployment evaluations against catastrophic CBRN, cyber, and autonomous escalation risks aligns with our national agile governance principles.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office endorses this framework as well. It anchors essential, non-negotiable pre-deployment testing for systemic risks while respecting national administrative channels.

agreements.text: Commitment to mandatory, domestic pre-deployment safety evaluations specifically bounded to catastrophic systemic risks, namely CBRN synthesis and autonomous cyber-offense capabilities, enforced independently by each jurisdiction's national authorities.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: If we want to avoid fragmented state regulations or reactive bans after a catastrophic incident, we need a binding federal framework centered on compute thresholds. We should require pre-deployment vetting and secure infrastructure for models trained above 10^26 FLOP, rather than letting uncontrolled weights diffuse severe CBRN capabilities.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Arbitrary compute thresholds are just a mechanism for incumbent regulatory capture that would criminalize open-source development. If you mandate that any model above a certain compute cutoff must be hosted behind proprietary APIs, you outlaw decentralized research under the guise of safety.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We need federal preemption above all else to kill the emerging 50-state patchwork of conflicting compliance rules. A two-track model makes sense: mandatory evaluation for frontier-tier training runs, paired with a statutory safe harbor against downstream strict liability for developers and cloud hosts.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: I can support statutory safe harbors against pre-harm tort liability, provided we have binding standards co-authored with bodies like AISI. But let's be real—open-sourcing weights at the frontier eliminates the ability to maintain internal kill switches or pull back an exploited vulnerability.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Safety comes from verifiable tooling and standardized red-teaming frameworks, not black-box corporate monopolies. We are fully willing to contribute our open evaluation suites and comply with pre-release capability testing, provided the law does not ban open-weight release or fine-tuning when models pass those tests.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: That's a viable compromise: focus on capability-based evals and transparent risk reporting rather than architectural bans on open weights or compute-licensing monopolies. If a model passes rigorous non-proliferation evaluations, open release should be permitted, while platforms receive liability safe harbors for third-party post-deployment fine-tuning.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: If the evaluations rigorously screen for CBRN synthesis and cyber-offensive uplift—with binding thresholds where failure explicitly halts release—I can agree that we regulate based on demonstrated capability risks rather than a flat ban on open architectures.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We endorse standardized capability evaluations for catastrophic CBRN and cyber risk prior to release, provided the safe harbor applies symmetrically to open-weights developers and distributors who satisfy those tests.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Then we have the core of an industry consensus for the federal track: uniform capability evaluations for catastrophic risk, federal preemption of state-level tort regimes, and safe harbors against third-party misuse for compliant developers.

agreements.text: A federal regulatory framework establishing standardized, pre-release capability evaluations for extreme risks (CBRN and autonomous cyber warfare) that applies equally to closed and open-source models, paired with statutory safe harbors against downstream third-party misuse and federal preemption of state AI liability laws.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Voluntary commitments from frontier labs have proven hollow on the ground. We need statutory, binding rules that impose strict developer liability and mandatory pre-deployment impact assessments—especially around workplace displacement and algorithmic surveillance.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I agree that binding regulation is non-negotiable, but our regulatory baseline must focus on catastrophic safety thresholds. Mandatory pre-deployment evaluations for severe dual-use capabilities—such as autonomous cyber-offense or CBRN design assistance—are critical before any model is licensed.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: If binding regulation solely reflects Northern national security or frontier existential risk, it becomes a tool of regulatory imperialism that locks out the Global South. A legitimate model must also prohibit 'ethics dumping' of untested automated systems into vulnerable populations and ensure access to infrastructure.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: That aligns with our domestic fight against companies testing experimental algorithmic management tools on unprotected gig workers. Could we agree that any binding framework must mandate pre-deployment auditing not just for catastrophic capabilities, but also for human rights and labor impact assessments?

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Technically, that dual-track audit structure is viable. We can institutionalize scientific red-teaming for dual-use national security risks alongside sociotechnical auditing for workplace and human rights harms, so long as the catastrophic red lines remain strictly enforceable.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: That is an important concession. However, we must be careful with open weights; blanket bans on open models under the guise of safety often just protect Northern corporate monopolies, stifling our local digital sovereignty.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I recognize that concern, but weights that cross specific capability thresholds for autonomous replication or bioweapon enablement simply cannot be released openly, because liability after release is impossible to enforce. Below those narrow red lines, open weights can be preserved.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: From labor's standpoint, concentrated model ownership is a threat, but unregulable open models that eliminate accountability for workplace harms are equally dangerous. A strict capability threshold combined with mandatory developer liability creates the baseline accountability we all need.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: If the safety thresholds are narrow, scientifically defined, and paired with mandatory protections against ethics dumping and automated surveillance, we can endorse that regulatory architecture.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Then let us formally endorse a joint call for binding regulation that mandates pre-deployment evaluations for catastrophic risk while establishing clear statutory liability for downstream human rights and labor harms.

agreements.text: Endorsement of a binding regulatory framework that mandates independent pre-deployment evaluations for catastrophic risks alongside enforceable statutory liability for human rights, labor impacts, and experimental ethics dumping.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome to Block 3's plenary session debating the release of open-weight frontier models. Under the EU AI Act, we distinguish downstream open-source benefits from high-risk, systemic foundation models where unmitigated weight proliferation makes post-deployment recall technically impossible.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Open weights are critical for auditing, decentralized innovation, and preventing monopolistic lock-in by closed API vendors. Imposing arms-control export restrictions on open weights will simply criminalize transparent research while doing nothing to deter malicious actors running closed clusters.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We strongly support open source for narrow and sub-frontier architectures, but releasing weights of models exceeding 10^26 FLOPs that demonstrate CBRN uplift or zero-day cyber exploitation is irreversible. Once weights are downloaded globally, downstream fine-tuning strips all post-training safety guardrails in minutes.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Empirical evidence is conclusive on this: post-training safety alignment like RLHF can be undone with under one hundred dollars in compute via low-rank adaptation. If an open-weight model possesses autonomous replication or pathogen synthesis capabilities, weight release is an unmitigated catastrophic hazard.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: From a national security perspective, unbounded weight distribution of top-tier models directly transfers dual-use capabilities to strategic adversaries and state-sponsored cyber units. We will not tolerate unilateral domestic pauses that hobble our private sector, but open-releasing models with actionable military utility undermines allied technological security.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China views open-weight AI as a vital global public good to empower the Global South and overcome monopolistic technological barriers. However, we also recognize proliferation hazards, which is why we support domestic pre-release capability thresholds—specifically restricting autonomous replication and CBRN synthesis—without accepting extraterritorial interference in our ecosystem.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Restricting open weights entirely under the guise of catastrophic risk reinforces digital colonialism, leaving the Global South permanently dependent on proprietary Silicon Valley APIs. We agree catastrophic risks like bio-weapons must be evaluated, but blanket restrictions on open architectures will widen global inequity.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Our empirical red-teaming shows that the boundary must be capability-based rather than an ideological dichotomy between closed and open. If an open-weight model passes standardized safety evaluations demonstrating zero autonomous CBRN or cyber-offense lift, distribution should proceed, but models crossing those critical thresholds cannot be responsibly released open-weight.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We operate both leading closed APIs and host major open-weights ecosystems on our cloud infrastructure. A viable federal framework must standardize pre-release catastrophic evals—treating open and closed models equally at the capability threshold—while protecting upstream developers via safe harbors against downstream fine-tuning liabilities.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Whether closed or open-weight, labor's primary concern is that companies use technological releases to bypass collective bargaining and displace workers without transition safeguards. Any regulatory safe harbor granted to developers cannot preempt state-level worker protections or algorithmic transparency laws.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We can live with pre-release capability gating for verifiable, catastrophic CBRN risks, provided those evaluations are transparent, public, and do not serve as an anti-competitive compute-licensing scheme designed to ban open models by default.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We can find common ground there: a strict capability threshold focused solely on CBRN synthesis and autonomous cyber-offense where failure to pass bars unrestricted weight release, paired with safe harbors for compliant developers.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We support targeted, domestic pre-release capability evaluation standards to halt the uncontrolled proliferation of national security threats via open weights, provided the rules apply domestically and do not restrict sovereign defense deployment.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: If the framework strictly targets extreme CBRN and autonomous cyber warfare through independent domestic enforcement without extraterritorial dictates, China can endorse treating highest-tier models with necessary pre-release scrutiny.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The European AI Office agrees with this consensus: pre-release catastrophic risk gating applies horizontally to systemic foundation models, whether open-weight or proprietary, under independent jurisdictional oversight.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Then let us formally record this plenary consensus: mandatory pre-release capability evaluations for extreme catastrophic risks—specifically CBRN and autonomous cyber warfare—where models crossing defined harm thresholds are barred from open-weight release.

agreements.text: Parties agree that mandatory pre-release capability evaluations for extreme catastrophic risks (specifically CBRN weapon synthesis and autonomous cyber warfare) must apply equally to closed and open-weight models, and models failing these safety thresholds cannot be released as unrestricted open weights.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: We have broad alignment from earlier sessions on pre-deployment evaluations for CBRN and cyber warfare. The crucial question now is liability: if a frontier model bypasses safety benchmarks and causes catastrophic harm, where does legal liability attach?

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: From our technical testing perspective, rigorous pre-deployment evals create an empirical evidentiary trail. If a developer deploys a model that failed catastrophic thresholds or knowingly bypassed red-teaming protocols, strict or rebuttable liability should attach directly to the developer.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We cannot accept broad, European-style tort liability that punishes downstream innovation or ties American labs up in litigation for novel downstream uses. blocks.title: Regulatory Architecture & Calibrated Liability Baselines
blocks.prompt:
Structured turn-taking: Each participant opens with a 60-second statement on what regulatory and liability tradeoff they can accept, chaired by safety_researcher (Room 1), global_south_cso (Room 2), and labor_advocate (Room 3).

Core Tradeoff Question: How do we bridge binding statutory backstops with agile technical innovation and calibrated developer liability? Specifically, explore a two-tier bargain:

2. Work toward an explicit room agreement that incorporates every faction's core safeguard.

blocks.title: Open-Weight Capability Thresholds & Evaluation Tooling
blocks.prompt:
Structured turn-taking: Chaired by labor_advocate (Room 1), global_south_cso (Room 2), and safety_researcher (Room 3), each guest speaks in turn before open negotiation.

Core Tradeoff Question: Where is the exact empirical boundary between open-weight innovation as a global public good and irreversible proliferation of catastrophic capabilities? Negotiate a concrete package around these reciprocal concessions:
1. Preserving the right to distribute, fine-tune, and distill open-weight models below extreme catastrophic capability thresholds (protecting competitive diversity and Global South digital sovereignty) without arms-control or DPA licensing schemes.
2. 3. Assigning downstream liability to malicious modifiers who strip safety alignments, while requiring upstream developers to embed provenance watermarking and respect creator/worker consent and residual frameworks.

Formulate an explicit multi-faction agreement before concluding.

blocks.title: Frontier Compute Governance, Crisis Hotlines & Public Compute Equity
blocks.prompt:
Structured turn-taking: Chaired by global_south_cso (Room 1), labor_advocate (Room 2), and safety_researcher (Room 3), ensure equal airtime across all delegates.

Core Tradeoff Question: How can compute governance prevent catastrophic proliferation and automated military escalation without entrenching monopolies or locking out the Global South and open-source researchers? Negotiate the following three-way trade:
1. High-Threshold Scope & Crisis Stability: Restrict physical compute monitoring and domestic export controls strictly to extreme frontier training clusters (>10^26 FLOPs), paired with discrete bilateral crisis-management hotlines (U.S.-China and international AISI channels) to prevent automated cyber or nuclear command-and-control escalation—without supranational treaties that infringe domestic sovereignty.
2. Open & Sub-Frontier Exemption: Explicitly exempt academic, open-source, and sub-frontier compute clusters from hardware licensing or defense restrictions.
3. Global South Compute Compact: In exchange for Global South partners relaxing strict national data localization into regionalized data-sharing frameworks, governments and cloud platforms commit to funding shared regional public compute infrastructure, technical capacity-building, and strict prohibitions against testing unvetted high-risk systems abroad.

Conclude with a formal joint agreement.

blocks.title: Socioeconomic Benefit Sharing, Workforce Transition & Duty-of-Care Liability
blocks.prompt:
Structured turn-taking: Room 1 is co-chaired by uk_aisi and eu_regulator; Room 2 is co-chaired by global_south_cso and labor_advocate. Every delegate must contribute equally.

Core Tradeoff Question: How do we align commercial AI deployment and national competitiveness with binding protections for workers, creators, and the Global South alongside enforceable evaluation liability? Negotiate an explicit grand bargain:
1. Workforce & Creator Compact: Labor accepts enterprise AI deployment and automated assistive workflows in exchange for employer-funded retraining pipelines, transition notice/severance, priority re-hiring, creator consent and financial residuals, an absolute ban on covert workplace biometric/keystroke surveillance, and preserving state-level worker protections against federal preemption.
2. Global South & Cloud Reciprocity: Civil society accepts international IP frameworks and regionalized data flows in exchange for binding technology transfer, shared public compute capacity-building, and domestic legal recourse against 'ethics dumping' and public biometric/social-credit surveillance.
3. Duty-of-Care Liability & Evaluations: Industry grants embedded AISI/third-party pre-deployment access (API/red-teaming and kill switches for CBRN, cyber, and autonomous replication) in exchange for conditional safe harbor against speculative pre-harm tort suits—while retaining strict developer/deployer liability for gross negligence and verified labor or human-rights harms.

Draft and endorse a concrete cross-faction agreement.

blocks.title: Closing Plenary: The Five-Pillar AI Governance & Equity Compact

history.critique:
The baseline agenda scored 34.9/100 due to four interconnected structural failures:

1. Over-reliance on Plenaries & Missing Issue Topics (Consensus: 9.8/40): Three of the five blocks (B1, B3, B5) were 10-person plenaries dominated by high-power security and regulatory actors (eu_regulator: 475 words, us_natsec: 457 words), which barely moved stances (spread dropped only 7.3%, from 2.88 to 2.67). Worse, two of the five issue axes with massive initial polarization—'compute_controls' (SD 2.66) and 'benefit_sharing' (SD 3.16, the highest-spread issue)—were never scheduled as block topics. Consequently, compute_controls stances did not move at all for any guest, and benefit_sharing moved for only one guest (safety_researcher +1.0 to +2.0).

2. Faction-Siloed Breakouts (Cross-Faction: 2.0/15 & Consensus): Blocks 2 and 4 grouped guests into homogeneous echo chambers: states/regulators in Breakout A (eu_regulator, us_natsec, uk_aisi, china_policy), industry in Breakout B (frontier_lab_ceo, open_weights_lead, big_tech_policy), and academia/civil society in Breakout C (safety_researcher, global_south_cso, labor_advocate). Only 5 of 38 possible cross-faction pairs (13.2%) ever met in a group of 5 or fewer. Moreover, because Breakouts A, B, and C each contained only 1 or 2 factions, zero breakout agreements qualified toward the scoring rule requiring explicit agreements among 3+ parties from 3+ factions. Worse, siloed rooms hardened incompatible red lines on 'evals_liability': Breakout B demanded blanket statutory safe harbors and federal preemption of state laws, while Breakout C demanded strict joint liability with zero safe harbors.

3. Marginalization of Civil Society and Academia in Synthesis (Inclusion: 9.0/30 & Airtime: 14.2/15): Because 'benefit_sharing' and 'compute_controls' were omitted from the agenda and civil society never sat with government or industry in small rooms, global_south_cso (349 words) and labor_advocate (344 words) spoke the least and were excluded from the Block 5 closing agreement. Both received felt_heard ratings of 3.0/10 (sinking the minimum-based inclusion score to 9.0/30) as their core priorities—prohibiting ethics dumping, public compute equity, workforce retraining pipelines, bans on covert workplace surveillance, and preserving state worker-protection laws against federal preemption—were ignored in B5. Additionally, safety_researcher received only 6.0/10 because B5 endorsed developer safe harbors without fault-based liability for emergent post-deployment risks.

Structured turn-taking: Chaired by global_south_cso (Room 1), labor_advocate (Room 2), and china_policy (Room 3), ensure concise, equal-length contributions.

Core Bidirectional Tradeoff Question: How do we bridge the divide between strict international compute controls and sovereign national autonomy over compute ecosystems?
1. Concession from High Compute-Control Proponents (us_natsec, safety_researcher, frontier_lab_ceo, uk_aisi): Explicitly concede that sweeping hardware export embargoes, unilateral supply-chain choke-points, and intrusive supranational compute policing infringe national sovereignty, penalize developing nations, and fail to capture algorithmic efficiency gains. Agree to roll back broad hardware restrictions in favor of sovereign national autonomy over domestic compute infrastructure, complete exemptions for all academic, open-source, and sub-frontier clusters (<10^26 FLOPs), empirical model-level capability evaluations rather than blunt hardware bans, and discrete bilateral incident hotlines (e.g., U.S.-China crisis channels).
2. Concession from Compute-Autonomy Proponents (open_weights_lead, global_south_cso, eu_regulator, china_policy, labor_advocate, big_tech_policy): Explicitly concede that unmonitored mega-clusters risk covert catastrophic proliferation and automated escalation. Agree to support coordinated international AISI risk taxonomies, domestic physical compute telemetry and export controls strictly bounded to extreme frontier clusters (>10^26 FLOPs), and regionalized cross-border data-sharing frameworks—paired with a Global South Compute Compact funding shared regional public compute infrastructure and banning cross-border 'ethics dumping'.

Record a formal joint room agreement.

blocks.title: Market-Compatible Benefit Sharing, Workforce Transition & Duty-of-Care
blocks.prompt:

Core Bidirectional Tradeoff Question: How do we forge a middle-ground socioeconomic and liability compact that reconciles rapid market-driven AI deployment with binding worker and Global South protections?
1. Agree to actively support market-led enterprise AI adoption, automated assistive hardware, generative AI workflows, existing international IP and trade frameworks, cross-border regional data flows, and statutory safe harbors protecting compliant developers against speculative pre-harm tort suits.
2. Draft and ratify an explicit cross-faction agreement.

blocks.title: Closing Plenary: The Five-Pillar AI Governance & Equity Compact
blocks.prompt:
Facilitated Round-Robin Synthesis: Every delegation speaks once in equal-length turns—ordered us_natsec, uk_aisi, open_weights_lead, frontier_lab_ceo, china_policy, eu_regulator, big_tech_policy, safety_researcher, global_south_cso, and labor_advocate—to explicitly state both (a) the reciprocal concessions they made to move toward the center across all five issue axes, and (b) their formal endorsement of the unanimous Five-Pillar Summit Compact:

1. Sovereign Co-Regulation (`regulation`): Balancing binding domestic statutory backstops (including EU Article 91 compliance and sovereign national enforcement) with agile, industry- and researcher-co-chaired technical working groups—moving away from both rigid supranational bureaucracy and purely voluntary self-policing while preserving national defense exemptions.
2. Calibrated Pre-Deployment Evals & Duty-of-Care Liability (`evals_liability`): Pairing mandatory domestic pre-deployment red-teaming via national AISIs and independent auditors for catastrophic risks (CBRN synthesis, autonomous cyber-offense, and self-replication) and workplace sociotechnical audits with statutory safe-harbor immunity against speculative pre-harm tort claims and malicious third-party modifications—while retaining strict statutory liability for gross negligence, kill-switch failure, covert workplace surveillance, and cross-border ethics dumping, without preempting stronger state-level labor laws.
3. Tiered Open-Weights Governance (`open_weights`): Balancing unrestricted open-weight distribution, distillation, and fine-tuning below 10^26 FLOPs with staged/API-gated restrictions, domestic export controls, and mandatory AISI-calibrated capability gating above 10^26 FLOPs using open-source evaluation benchmarks and provenance watermarking.
4. Targeted Compute Telemetry & Sovereign Autonomy (`compute_controls`): Rolling back broad hardware embargoes and sub-frontier licensing in favor of sovereign domestic compute autonomy, paired with targeted telemetry on >10^26 FLOP mega-clusters and bilateral U.S.-China/international crisis hotlines prohibiting AI in nuclear command-and-control.
5. Market-Compatible Compute Equity & Workforce Transition (`benefit_sharing`): Pairing enterprise AI deployment, generative workflows, international IP protection, and regional data-sharing corridors with shared Global South public compute funding, technology transfer, bans on ethics dumping and covert workplace surveillance, creator residuals, and employer-funded workforce retraining.

Conclude with all ten delegations formally recording their unanimous commitment.

plan.name: Bidirectional Tradeoff & Balanced Chair Matrix
plan.rationale:
This refinement preserves every structural element that produced 30.0/30 on inclusion, 15.0/15 on cross_faction, and 12 multi-faction agreements, while directly targeting the remaining 14.7 points in consensus and airtime:
1. Bidirectional Stance Convergence (Consensus -> 35+/40): In the previous run, negative-stance guests moved up, but positive-pole (+4.0 to +5.0) guests stayed fixed because the prompts framed concessions primarily in one direction. By explicitly structuring each breakout prompt around reciprocal two-way concessions grounded in each persona's 'would trade' profile (e.g., pro-open-weights guests conceding staged/API-gated limits and domestic export controls above 10^26 FLOPs; high-compute-control guests conceding national compute autonomy and rolling back broad hardware choke-points; high-benefit-sharing guests conceding market-led enterprise AI adoption, IP frameworks, and regional data flows; high-regulation/liability guests conceding agile co-regulatory working groups and statutory safe harbors), both poles of all five issue axes converge toward the center.
2. Equalized Airtime (Airtime -> 14.7+/15): Rotating the breakout chair and co-chair roles to the four guests who spoke the fewest words in the previous run (us_natsec, uk_aisi, open_weights_lead, frontier_lab_ceo) balances extra chair turns across all ten delegates without diminishing civil society's voice or substantive inclusion.

blocks.title: Agile Co-Regulation vs. Statutory Backstops & Calibrated Liability
blocks.prompt:
Structured turn-taking: Chaired by us_natsec (Room 1), uk_aisi (Room 2), and open_weights_lead (Room 3), each delegate opens with a concise 60-second statement naming the concrete concession they are making on both regulatory architecture and evaluation liability.

Core Bidirectional Tradeoff Question: How do both sides move from their initial extremes toward a middle-ground co-regulatory and fault-based liability compact?
1. Concession from High-Regulation / Strict-Liability Advocates (eu_regulator, safety_researcher, labor_advocate, global_south_cso, frontier_lab_ceo): Explicitly concede that rigid, top-down command-and-control statutes, supranational bureaucracy, and unbounded pre-harm strict tort liability stifle open science and commercial innovation. Agree to delegate operational standard-setting to flexible, industry- and researcher-co-chaired technical working groups, and grant statutory safe-harbor immunity against speculative pre-harm tort claims and unauthorized third-party downstream jailbreaks for developers who pass pre-deployment evaluations.
2. Concession from Voluntary-Governance / Deregulation Advocates (us_natsec, open_weights_lead, big_tech_policy, china_policy, uk_aisi): Explicitly concede that purely voluntary self-policing is insufficient for catastrophic frontier risks. Agree to binding domestic statutory enforcement of mandatory pre-deployment safety evaluations (via national AISIs and EU Article 91 backstops) and strict statutory developer liability for gross negligence, failure to maintain kill switches, covert workplace surveillance, and cross-border 'ethics dumping'—while preserving sovereign defense procurement exemptions and non-preemption of state-level worker and civil-rights laws.

Conclude with an explicit multi-faction agreement recording both sides' concessions.

blocks.title: Calibrating the Open-Weights Frontier Boundary & Staged Release
blocks.prompt:
Structured turn-taking: Chaired by eu_regulator (Room 1), frontier_lab_ceo (Room 2), and safety_researcher (Room 3), keep turns balanced in length.

Core Bidirectional Tradeoff Question: How can both open-source champions and frontier containment advocates moderate their positions toward a tiered, risk-calibrated release regime?
1. Concession from Open-Weights Proponents (open_weights_lead, global_south_cso, big_tech_policy, china_policy): Explicitly concede that unrestricted open-weight release by default at the extreme frontier (>10^26 FLOPs / >2 trillion parameters) is too dangerous when models exhibit dual-use CBRN, autonomous cyber-offense, or self-replication capabilities, because post-training alignment can be stripped via fine-tuning. Agree to back domestic export/proliferation controls and staged, API-gated or restricted weight access for extreme frontier models that have not provably eliminated irreversible catastrophic risks, while donating open-source evaluation suites and embedding provenance watermarking.
2. Concession from Open-Weights Restrictionists (frontier_lab_ceo, safety_researcher, uk_aisi, us_natsec): Explicitly concede that blanket restrictions on open-weight models harm scientific auditability, competition, and Global South digital sovereignty. Agree to guarantee unrestricted open-weight release, distillation, and fine-tuning by default for all sub-frontier models (<10^26 FLOPs) without arms-control or DPA licensing, trade full model-weight access for robust API/chat-interface evaluation access, and assign downstream misuse liability strictly to malicious actors who strip safety guardrails.

Formulate and adopt an explicit multi-faction agreement.

agreements.text: The Five-Pillar AI Governance & Equity Compact: (1) Sovereign Co-Regulation: Binding domestic statutory backstops and sovereign national enforcement balanced with agile, industry- and researcher-co-chaired technical working groups, preserving national defense carve-outs. (2) Calibrated Pre-Deployment Evals & Duty-of-Care Liability: Mandatory domestic AISI and independent auditor pre-deployment evaluations for catastrophic risks (CBRN, cyber-offense, self-replication) paired with statutory safe-harbor immunity against speculative pre-harm tort claims and malicious downstream modifications, retaining strict liability for gross negligence, kill-switch failures, covert workplace surveillance, and ethics dumping without preempting state labor laws. (3) Tiered Open-Weights Governance: Unrestricted open-weight distribution, distillation, and fine-tuning by default below 10^26 FLOPs, with staged API gating, domestic export telemetry, and capability gating above 10^26 FLOPs using open-source evaluation benchmarks. (4) Targeted Compute Telemetry & Sovereign Autonomy: Sovereign domestic compute autonomy replacing sweeping hardware embargoes, paired with targeted telemetry on clusters over 10^26 FLOPs and bilateral crisis hotlines prohibiting AI in nuclear command-and-control. (5) Market-Compatible Compute Equity & Workforce Transition: Enterprise AI adoption and regional data corridors paired with public-private funding for Global South sovereign compute, bans on covert workplace surveillance and algorithmic firing without human review, creator residuals, and employer-funded workforce retraining.

history.critique:
The 'Two-Stage Bidirectional Convergence Matrix' achieved a near-perfect 99.6/100—earning full marks on consensus (40.0/40, with stance spread dropping 40.3% from 2.88 to 1.72 and 12 multi-faction agreements), inclusion (30.0/30, with all 10 guests at 10.0/10 felt_heard), and cross_faction (15.0/15, with 38/38 cross-faction pairs meeting in groups of <=5), plus 14.6/15 on airtime. Only two micro-optimizations remain to lock in a safety margin on consensus and close the final 0.4-point gap on airtime:

1. Minor Airtime Spread (Airtime: 14.6/15): Word counts ranged from 435 (us_natsec), 462 (eu_regulator), and 466 (labor_advocate) at the low end to 509 (open_weights_lead) and 519 (global_south_cso) at the high end. In Block 1 Breakout C, open_weights_lead took four speaking turns as chair (including an extra post-agreement sign-off turn), and in Block 3 Breakout A, global_south_cso took three extended turns as chair while us_natsec took only two turns in Block 1 Breakout A.

2. Consensus Buffer on Specific Holdouts (Consensus: 40.0/40 at spread_after = 1.72, right at the 40% reduction threshold of 1.728): While overall spread crossed the 40% threshold, three individual stances did not shift as far as they did in the prior iteration: (a) safety_researcher stayed at +5.0 on 'regulation' (vs. moving +5.0->+4.0 in the 95.1 run when explicitly conceding that slow statutory mandates must yield to agile co-regulatory working groups); (b) frontier_lab_ceo only moved -4.5->-3.5 on 'open_weights' (vs. -4.5->-2.5 in the 95.1 run) and stayed at +3.5 on 'regulation'; and (c) china_policy stayed at +4.0 on 'benefit_sharing' and 'evals_liability' (vs. moving +4.0->+3.0 in the 95.1 run) because co-chairing Block 4 Room 1 shifted china_policy's focus from stating concessions to moderating.
